triage.name: Marasmus
triage.reason: Severe wasting from inadequate energy intake; diagnosis is clinical from growth and dietary history with a recognizable exam.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'Chest x-ray' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if respiratory symptoms or suspected tuberculosis)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Blood culture' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if fever, hypothermia, or signs of sepsis)
auto-repaired: workup: 'Stool culture' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if diarrhea with blood or persistent diarrhea)
auto-repaired: workup: 'HIV test' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if risk factors or recurrent infections)

auto-repaired: workup: 'Tuberculosis testing (IGRA or tuberculin skin test)' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if exposure, chronic cough, or failure to improve with feeding)

demographics: Most common in low-resource and food-insecure settings
Classically affects infants and young children during or after weaning

risk_factors.text: Inadequate total energy intake over weeks to months
Early cessation of breastfeeding without adequate replacement
Recurrent infections such as diarrhea or pneumonia
Underlying chronic illness with increased metabolic demand or malabsorption
Neglect or inability of caregivers to feed the child

chief_complaints.text: My child is not gaining weight and looks very thin
My child seems weak and is less active than before
My child's skin is loose and hangs in folds

hpi.onset: Gradual, over weeks to months as intake remains inadequate
hpi.duration: Weeks to months before medical attention is sought
hpi.progression: Progressive weight loss and wasting; initially a well-nourished child becomes visibly thin, then weak and listless
hpi.quality: Not applicable; weight loss and wasting predominate
hpi.severity: Severe by the time of diagnosis; marked wasting

associated_symptoms.text: Loss of body fat and muscle
Fever when an infection is present

pertinent_negatives: Swelling of the feet, legs, or face (edema)
Fever without another source of infection
Severe vomiting as the main problem
Preserved normal growth until a brief recent illness

atypical.how_it_differs: Wasting often occurs in the setting of self-neglect, dementia, depression, or malignancy; there is no growth chart to demonstrate failure to thrive, and it may be mistaken for cachexia or sarcopenia.
missing_classic_features: Failure to thrive on growth curve

general.mild: Appears thin but alert and interactive; may be quiet but not ill-looking.
general.moderate: Markedly thin with loose skin; apathetic, less active, but responsive to caregiver.
general.severe: Emaciated, weak, listless; may be hypothermic; prominent bones and sunken cheeks; requires careful handling.
general.critical: Moribund, lethargic or unresponsive; signs of shock, severe hypothermia; immediate stabilization needed.

findings.maneuver: Weigh the child and plot weight-for-length or BMI on WHO growth chart
findings.finding: Weight-for-length or BMI below expected; severe wasting if below -3 z-score

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, buttocks, and extremities; pinch skin over triceps
findings.finding: Loss of subcutaneous fat with thin, loose skin over cheeks and buttocks

findings.maneuver: Palpate the deltoid, thigh, and buttocks
findings.finding: Marked muscle wasting with prominent bones

findings.maneuver: Gently lift a fold of skin over the abdomen or thigh
findings.finding: Skin lifts easily and returns slowly due to loss of subcutaneous tissue
Abdomen may be distended but soft, with visible bowel loops

findings.maneuver: Inspect hair color, texture, and ease of plucking
findings.finding: Hair is thin, dry, dull, and easily plucked; may have color changes

findings.maneuver: Observe interaction with caregiver and environment
findings.finding: Irritable, apathetic, or listless; may be lethargic in severe cases

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of the feet, hands, and periorbital area
Palpate the liver edge below the right costal margin

labs.caveat: Anemia is common in marasmus; may be normocytic or microcytic if iron deficiency coexists.
Leukopenia can occur due to immune dysfunction; infection may not produce the expected leukocytosis.
Hypoglycemia may be asymptomatic; check before feeds.
Serum potassium may be low or normal despite total body depletion.
Hypophosphatemia often appears or worsens during refeeding.
Hypomagnesemia can cause cardiac arrhythmias and seizures.
Albumin is often normal in pure marasmus; a low value suggests infection or overlap with kwashiorkor.
Low BUN reflects low protein intake and reduced muscle mass.
Low creatinine from reduced muscle mass can mask renal impairment.
Hyponatremia may be due to excess free water or impaired renal handling.

findings.finding: Flattened T waves or prominent U waves

imaging.preferred_when: Respiratory symptoms or suspected tuberculosis or pneumonia

findings.text: Hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy suggesting tuberculosis

initial.why: Screen for anemia, leukopenia, and infection
Check glucose, electrolytes, and kidney function
Check albumin and total protein; screen for liver involvement

supporting.why: Helps detect occult infection or systemic inflammation

supporting.only_if: fever, hypothermia, or signs of sepsis
diarrhea with blood or persistent diarrhea

supporting.why: HIV infection can cause severe malnutrition

supporting.test: Tuberculosis testing (IGRA or tuberculin skin test)
supporting.only_if: exposure, chronic cough, or failure to improve with feeding

not_indicated.why: No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Not indicated when inadequate intake is obvious; reserve for failure to thrive without clear cause

decision_points: Check point-of-care glucose in every severely malnourished child before feeds
Correct hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and dehydration before starting feeds
Check and replete potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus before and during refeeding to prevent refeeding syndrome
Obtain a chest x-ray and consider infection workup if fever or respiratory signs are present
Do not rely on serum albumin to rule out marasmus; it may be normal

criteria.name: Severe acute malnutrition (marasmus)
criteria.summary: Clinical diagnosis of severe wasting due to inadequate energy intake.
items: Weight-for-length/height z-score below -3 SD of WHO growth standards
Mid-upper arm circumference <115 mm in children 6–59 months
Visible severe wasting of fat and muscle

differential.name: Kwashiorkor
differential.why_considered: Both are severe protein-energy malnutrition and can occur in the same food-insecure setting.
differential.trigger: Presence of edema, skin changes, or a dietary history that is low in protein but not necessarily low in calories.

history: Diet more deficient in protein than total energy
Rapid weaning to a low-protein staple
Preceding infection such as measles or diarrhea
exam: Pitting edema of feet, legs, hands, and face
labs: Low serum albumin and total protein
Weight-for-length often higher than marasmus for the same degree of illness
imaging: Not needed for diagnosis; ultrasound may show fatty liver

differential.name: HIV infection
differential.why_considered: Chronic viral infection can cause severe wasting and failure to thrive, especially in infants.
differential.trigger: Recurrent or opportunistic infections, known maternal HIV, or failure to improve with adequate feeding.

history: Failure to thrive despite adequate food intake
Known maternal HIV or high-risk exposure
labs: Positive HIV antibody/antigen test or DNA PCR
imaging: Not routinely diagnostic; may show pneumonia or other opportunistic infection

differential.name: Tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic infection can cause severe wasting and failure to thrive.
differential.trigger: Chronic cough, known TB contact, or failure to improve with nutritional support.

history: Chronic cough for more than 2-3 weeks
Failure to gain weight despite feeding
labs: Positive tuberculin skin test or IGRA
Gastric aspirate or sputum AFB positive
imaging: Chest x-ray with hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, infiltrate, or miliary pattern

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic malabsorption can cause wasting and failure to thrive, especially after gluten introduction.

imaging: Not diagnostically useful; duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy

differential.name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Weight loss and fatigue can occur in children, but with polyuria and polydipsia.

history: No clear history of inadequate intake
exam: No severe loss of subcutaneous fat

differential.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential.why_considered: Pancreatic insufficiency and chronic lung disease can cause failure to thrive and wasting.

imaging: Chest x-ray may show hyperinflation and bronchiectasis

severity.mild: Early wasting with weight-for-length or BMI falling across percentiles; child remains alert and interactive, has no significant metabolic derangements, and can be managed with close outpatient feeding support.
severity.moderate: Marked wasting with loose skin and decreased subcutaneous fat; child is apathetic or less active, may have mild anemia, electrolyte deficits, or low albumin; requires structured nutritional rehabilitation and monitoring.
severity.severe: Severe wasting with weight-for-length/height z-score below -3, obvious muscle and fat loss, lethargy, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, and significant electrolyte abnormalities; needs inpatient stabilization with careful refeeding.
severity.critical: Life-threatening malnutrition with lethargy/unresponsiveness, shock, severe hypothermia, severe hypoglycemia, or cardiac arrhythmia; immediately life-threatening and requires emergency metabolic and hemodynamic support.

red_flags.finding: Edema of feet, hands, or face
red_flags.meaning: Points to kwashiorkor or another cause; requires albumin and careful fluid management
Severe hypothermia; increases mortality and signals impaired metabolic regulation
Hypoglycemia, sepsis, or severe electrolyte disturbance; needs immediate glucose and evaluation
Hypoglycemia can cause seizures and brain injury; treat immediately
Cardiac conduction risk; may precede arrhythmia, especially during refeeding

red_flags.finding: Low potassium, magnesium, or phosphorus before or during feeding
red_flags.meaning: Refeeding syndrome risk; correct electrolytes before advancing calories

red_flags.finding: Fever or hypothermia with ill appearance
red_flags.meaning: Occult infection; malnourished children may not mount fever or leukocytosis

red_flags.finding: Poor weight gain despite a supervised adequate diet
red_flags.meaning: Consider malabsorption, HIV, tuberculosis, or other chronic disease

complications.name: Refeeding syndrome
clues: Sudden drop in phosphate, potassium, or magnesium after feeds

special_populations.differences: Highest risk during weaning; metabolic reserves are small, so hypoglycemia and hypothermia develop quickly. Use expressed breast milk or standard therapeutic feeds cautiously and monitor closely.
Under 5 use WHO weight-for-length/height and MUAC; older children use BMI-for-age. Any severe wasting is classified as severe acute malnutrition regardless of edema.
Wasting often reflects chronic disease, depression, or self-neglect; diagnose with BMI and history rather than growth charts, and refeeding syndrome risk is high.
Maternal calorie need is higher; severe malnutrition threatens both mother and fetus; involve obstetrics and nutrition early.
Suspect HIV/tuberculosis; infections may be atypical with less fever and leukocytosis; broad infection workup and early anti-infective treatment are needed.

key_questions.question: What has the child been eating and drinking each day?
key_questions.looking_for: Inadequate total calories for age: watery porridge, dilute formula, early weaning, or periods of little food.

key_questions.question: When did the weight loss or poor weight gain begin?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months, not days; weight-for-length falling across percentiles.

key_questions.question: Has the child had any swelling of the feet, legs, or face?
key_questions.looking_for: No edema; edema would suggest kwashiorkor or another cause.

key_questions.question: Has the child had diarrhea? If yes, how often and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Intermittent or chronic diarrhea that increases losses and may accompany infection.

key_questions.question: Has there been fever, cough, or trouble breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: No fever makes simple infection less likely; fever may point to tuberculosis, pneumonia, or sepsis.

key_questions.question: How is the child’s mood and activity level?
key_questions.looking_for: Apathy, irritability, or less active; severe lethargy suggests hypoglycemia or sepsis.

key_questions.question: Is there any vomiting?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually minimal; persistent vomiting suggests gastrointestinal pathology.

key_questions.question: What serious illnesses or hospitalizations has the child had?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent pneumonia, diarrhea, tuberculosis, or HIV infection that can cause or worsen wasting.

key_questions.question: Does the child have any known chronic diseases?
key_questions.looking_for: Malabsorption, congenital heart disease, kidney disease, or HIV that can cause failure to thrive.

key_questions.question: Does the family have reliable access to enough food and safe water?
key_questions.looking_for: Food insecurity, poverty, unclean water; informs diagnosis and safe discharge plan.

key_questions.question: Are there any concerns about the ability to feed the child?
key_questions.looking_for: Inadequate caregiver knowledge, neglect, or inability to prepare adequate food.

key_questions.question: Has the child become too sleepy or felt cold to touch?
key_questions.looking_for: Lethargy, hypothermia, or hypoglycemia requiring immediate treatment.

reasoning_points: Inadequate total energy intake over weeks to months with early weaning or food insecurity
Severe wasting: weight-for-length/height z-score below -3, mid-upper arm circumference <115 mm in children 6–59 months, or visible severe wasting
Loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle mass with loose skin folds and prominent bones
No nutritional edema, distinguishing marasmus from kwashiorkor
Child may be apathetic or irritable; severe lethargy is a red flag
Diarrhea and infections may be present and can worsen malnutrition
Check glucose and electrolytes before feeding; hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatemia are common
Serum albumin is often normal in marasmus

easy: Early weaning to watery cereal or dilute formula
Weight-for-length far below the third percentile with visible severe wasting
No edema, no fever, and alert
medium: Older child with food insecurity and chronic low-grade diarrhea
Caregiver underreports inadequate intake or shares household food with several siblings
Dyselectrolytemia requiring careful monitoring before refeeding
hard: Severely marasmic child with hypothermia, lethargy, and glucose below 45 mg/dL
Occult infection without fever or leukocytosis
Older adult with cachexia, depression, and self-neglect
